newsitem.title: THAILAND: TelecomAsia in drive to up revenue.
newsitem.headline: TelecomAsia in drive to up revenue.

text.p: Despite the current Thai economic crisis and the weakness of the baht, leading firm TelecomAsia Corp Plc plans to launch a new hand phone system in Bangkok later this year that could raise its revenues by about 50 percent.

Known as the Personal Communication Telephone (PCT) system, the service uses handsets that cost up to two-thirds less than conventional mobile phones, and are linked to the customer's fixed-line home telephone number installed by TelecomAsia.
TelecomAsia has spent about $5.0 billion on the installation of 2.6 million fixed lines allotted to it by the government in a 25-year concession that began in October 1992.
The installation of fixed lines covering Bangkok and three neighbouring provinces of Nonthaburi, Samut Prakan and Pathum Thani was completed last September.

"The PCT system, which uses high technology from Japan, Germany and the U.S., will be introduced for the first time in Bangkok as well as in the world in the last quarter of this year," Supachai Chearavanont, executive vice president of TelecomAsia, told Reuters in an interview.

The PCT system will initially cover an area of 1,500 sq km in the Bangkok area. The company plans to cover the service for the entire 4,200 sq km (1,575 square mile) area in Bangkok and its three neighbouring provinces early next year, he said.

"TelecomAsia has invested about $500 million on PCT and it hopes to have its revenue rise about 50 percent from the system. We're hoping that about one million handsets would be sold to subscribers in the next two or three years," he said.
The company raked in total revenue in 1996 of 7.32 billion baht. Analysts said they expected TelecomAsia's revenue this year would be higher at around 12.17 billion baht.

"We consider the PCT as a value-added service on TA's fixed-line network and the main users will be housewives, students and middle-income earners. The subscription fee is cheaper than mobile phones, which suits them well while the economy fares rather poorly in the country," Supachai said.
Currently, subscribers for mobile phones will have to pay a monthly fee of 500 baht ($16.13 dollars) and a charge of three baht per minute.

On the PCT system, subscribers pay 300 baht, which includes 200 baht for the PCT and 100 baht for home telephone, each month. The company charges three baht for the first two minutes and 1.50 baht for the next minute.

Analysts said the firm appeared to be a good long-term investment because it was enlarging its investment in every kind of telecom project despite the baht's flotation on July 2 and subsequent de facto devaluation by over 20 percent.

"TA's executives don't care about investing money to expand its businesses as long as they can beat competitors. They could later increase prices of their products when they find their business competitors can't compete with them," said Somchai Wongrassamee, an analyst at Ekachart Finance and Securities.
Somchai said he expected the PCT would be welcomed by people in Bangkok.
The company's shares hit a year-low of 23.50 previously but the price closed up 3.75 baht at 44.75 on Monday.
